full_judgment:
10. After the close of the prosecution case, the learned Tribunal in consideration of the evidence on record as well as facts and circumstances of the case convicted the accused-petitioner and others for offence charged and sentenced them there under as above vide judgment and order dated 7-7-2008. 

 12. Mr Ahsanul Karim, the learned Advocate for the convict petitioner submits that there is no legal evidence to convict the petitioner, more so the initiation, continuation and conviction of the petitioner is barred by law: that section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires that the search and seizure of any material must be conducted in presence of two independent witnesses but in the instant case, there was no independent witness and the seizure list witness No. 1 is a fictitious person and did not give evidence and the PW6 and PW 15 are not credible independent witnesses and therefore, the seizure list has not been proved and the seizure list is inadmissible evidence, for which reason the seizure list is not legal evidence; that the evidence adduced by the prosecution, especially exhibit. No.9, 10 and 11 proves that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 can lawfully keep the alleged foreign currencies without giving any declaration and thereby there cannot be any violation or contravention of any provision of the act or rule, direction or order made thereunder and, as such, there being no contravention of Law. He further submits that the Tribunal for convicting the convict-petitioner merely relied on the fact that the accused Nos. 2 to 5 failed to show valid documents for keeping the said foreign currencies under their custody at the time of search and seizure without adverting to the documentary evidence but Exhibit Nos. 9, 10 and 11 which proves that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 can lawfully keep the said foreign currencies under their custody and that from the Exhibit-9 as adduced by the prosecution it appears that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 jointly kept foreign currencies equivalent to U$$ 20,857.79 whereas from exhibit-10 it appears that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 are entitled to keep U$$ 25000 jointly and therefore, it is proved from the documentary evidenced adduced by the prosecution that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 including the convict-petitioner did not keep more than Us 25,000 and, as such, they have not violated or contravened any provision of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 or any order of direction thereunder, and, as such, the charge against the convict-petitioner and others accused that they have committed offence under section 23 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 is not supported by any evidence whatsoever. He further submits that the said judgment dated 7-7- 2008 convicting and sentencing the convict petitioner is liable to be quashed since the said case has been initiated without jurisdiction and that cognizance of the said case has been taken without jurisdiction since neither the Government not Bangladesh Bank authorized the concerned SI to lodge the FIR for which reason the initiation and continuation of the proceeding of the case is barred by law. 

 15. Mr Md Shohrawardi, the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the State, on the other hand, submits that the convict-petitioner including others kept in their possession a huge amount of foreign currencies without any lawful authority and the convict petitioner and others failed to show any valid document for keeping those currencies in their possession and that the prosecution has proved the case adducing reliable evidence. 

 16. He further submits that the impugned judgment dated 7-7-2008 passed by the Metropolitan Special Tribunal No. 2 is based on legal evidence and that the application for quashment under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure has no substance and, as such, the application is liable to be rejected. 

 18. A convict may invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure if he can make out a case of "Coram non-judice" of the trial Court or that the facts alleged do not constitute any criminal offence or that the conviction has been based on no legal evidence or otherwise for securing the ends of justice. 

 19. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances of the case, let us examine the evidence on record and the relevant laws. 

 25. In the charge farmed against the accused persons, it is clearly stated that the seized foreign currencies were brought in valid way. It is the only allegation against the accused persons that they brought those Foreign Currencies for smuggling purpose. But scanning the evidence of PWs, we find no such evidence. There is no iota of evidence that they brought those foreign currencies for smuggling purpose. All PWs only stated that the accused persons failed to show any valid documents for keeping those foreign Currencies in their possession. The evidence adduced by the PWs are not relevant for proving the charge frame against the accused persons including the convict-petitioner. Hence it can be safely concluded that it is a case of no evidence. 

 26. Recovery and seizure are the main factors in this case. Now let us see whether the seizure was conducted and seizure list was prepared as per the provision of Law. Section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires that the search and seizure of any matter must be conducted in presence of two independent witnesses but in the instant case, there is no independent witness and the seizure list witness No.1 is a fictitious person who did not give evidence and the PW.6 and PW.15 are not credible and independent witnesses and therefore, the seizure list has not been proved and the said seizure list is inadmissible evidence for which reason the seizure list is not legal evidence. We find support of the above view in the case of Sobhan Ramjan vs State reported in 45 DLR 521. 

 Therefore, from the evidence adduced by the prosecution, it appears that the any of the accused Nos. 1 to 5 or the convict-petitioner is entitled to keep US$ 5000 without any declaration or permission of Bangladesh Bank and, as such, accused Nos. 1 to 5 including the convict petitioner are jointly entitled to keep up to the limit of US$ 25000 without any declaration. As such if the alleged foreign currencies do not exceed US$ 25000 then no provision of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 or any order or direction thereunder has been violated or contravened. In fact, the prosecution has not proved that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 jointly kept under their custody more than US$ 25000. The PW- 1 only deposed that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 jointly kept the said foreign currencies without deposing whether the said foreign currencies exceed US$ 25000. But from the Exhibit-9 as exhibited by the prosecution, it is proved that the foreign currencies seized by the prosecution do not exceed US$ 25000. From the Exhibit-9 as adduced by the prosecution it appears that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 jointly kept foreign currencies equivalent to US$ 20,8557.79. Whereas from Exhibit 10 it appears that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 are entitled to keep US$ 25000 jointly. Therefore, it is proved from the documentary evidence adduced by the prosecution that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 including the convict-petitioner did not keep more than US$ 25000 and, as such, they have not violated or contravened any provision of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 or any order of direction thereunder and since as per evidence of the prosecution the accused Nos. 1 to 5 including petitioner are jointly entitled to keep the said alleged foreign currencies which is equivalent to US$ 20,857.79 which is much below of US$ 25000. So the charge against the convict-petitioner and other accused that they have committed offence under section 23 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 is not supported by any evidence whatsoever. 

 35. Law permits that a person is authorized to keep up to US$ 5000. In the instant case there were 5 accused who jointly were authorized to hold US$ 25,000 Exhibit-9 prove that there were only US$ 20,857.79. Therefore, admittedly no offence has been committed. Bangladesh Bank by exhibit 10 confirms that up to US$ 5000 a person can legally keep. As stated above the total accused being five in number and they collectively can hold US$ 25,000. But since the. disputed currency collectively is less than that of U$ 25,000 no offences has been committed. Exhibit Nos. 9 and 10 as adduced by the prosecution as evidence does not support the prosecution case rather disproved the allegation of prosecution. None of the prosecution witnesses. deposed that the accused Nos. 1 to 5 have been holding more than U$ 25,000 and, as such, there is no legal evidence to sustain conviction neither the evidence adduced by the prosecution supports the conviction of the convict petitioner. 

 36. The critical analysis of the facts and circumstances of the case and of the aforesaid evidence clearly indicates that the prosecution has failed to prove the charge levlled against the convict-petitioner under section 23 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947.
